entries.1:1: This opens the story by announcing that the good news about Jesus, God's Son, is beginning. For the reader, it signals that what follows is meant to be received as genuinely good news from God.
entries.1:2: The writer quotes the prophet Isaiah to show that someone was promised long ago to prepare the way ahead of the Lord. It tells the reader that what is happening now was planned and foretold, not random.
entries.1:3: A voice in the wilderness calls people to get the road ready for the Lord. It means the reader should expect the Lord to arrive and should prepare their heart for him.
entries.1:4: John appeared in the wilderness baptizing people as an outward sign that they had turned from sin and were forgiven. It shows the reader that real change of heart, not just a ritual, is what matters.
entries.1:5: Crowds from all over Judea and Jerusalem went out to John, confessed their sins, and were baptized in the Jordan. It shows the reader how widely people sensed their need for a fresh start with God.
entries.1:6: John dressed in rough camel-hair clothing and ate locusts and wild honey, like an old-time prophet living simply. It tells the reader that his message mattered more than comfort or appearance.
entries.1:7: John told the crowds that someone far greater was coming after him, so great that John felt unworthy even to untie his sandals. It directs the reader's attention past John to Jesus.
entries.1:8: John explained that his water baptism was only a preparation; the coming one would baptize people with the Holy Spirit. It tells the reader that Jesus offers something deeper than an outward ceremony—God's own Spirit.
entries.1:9: Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. It shows the reader that Jesus chose to stand with ordinary people in their repentance.
entries.1:10: As Jesus came up from the water, he saw heaven opened and the Spirit descend on him like a dove. It tells the reader that God's Spirit was visibly on Jesus for the work ahead.
entries.1:11: A voice from heaven declared that Jesus is God's beloved Son, in whom God delights. It tells the reader who Jesus really is and that the Father's approval rests on him.
entries.1:12: Right after his baptism, the Spirit drove Jesus out into the wilderness. It shows the reader that God's leading can include hard, lonely places, not only mountaintop moments.
entries.1:13: Jesus spent forty days in the wilderness being tested by Satan, among wild animals, with angels caring for him. It tells the reader that Jesus faced real temptation and that God's care was with him.
entries.1:14: After John was imprisoned, Jesus began preaching God's good news in Galilee. It shows the reader that the message continued and moved forward even when John's work was cut short.
entries.1:15: Jesus announced that the time had come, God's kingdom was near, and people should turn from sin and believe the good news. It calls the reader to respond personally with repentance and faith.
entries.1:16: Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw Simon and Andrew, brothers who were fishermen, casting a net. It shows the reader that Jesus notices ordinary working people.
entries.1:17: Jesus invited them to follow him and promised to make them fishers of people. It tells the reader that following Jesus means being reshaped for a new purpose—helping others find him.
entries.1:18: They left their nets at once and followed him. It shows the reader that responding to Jesus can require immediate, wholehearted leaving behind.
entries.1:19: A little farther on, Jesus saw James and John, sons of Zebedee, mending their nets in their boat. It shows the reader that Jesus calls people in the middle of their everyday work.
entries.1:20: Jesus called them, and they left their father and the hired workers in the boat to follow him. It tells the reader that following Jesus may cost family ties and familiar security.
entries.1:21: They arrived at Capernaum, and on the Sabbath Jesus went into the synagogue and taught. It shows the reader that Jesus began his public work in ordinary places of worship.
entries.1:22: The people were amazed because Jesus taught with real authority, unlike the scribes. It tells the reader that Jesus' words carry weight and deserve serious attention.
entries.1:23: In the synagogue was a man controlled by an evil spirit, who cried out. It shows the reader that Jesus' authority would meet real spiritual opposition, not just ideas.
entries.1:24: The evil spirit recognized Jesus as the Holy One of God and asked whether he had come to destroy it. It tells the reader that even dark powers know who Jesus is, though they oppose him.
entries.1:25: Jesus sharply ordered the spirit to be quiet and come out of the man. It shows the reader that Jesus has authority over evil and silences it.
entries.1:26: The evil spirit shook the man violently, cried out loudly, and left him. It tells the reader that Jesus' command is effective, even when the struggle looks messy.
entries.1:27: Everyone was astonished and asked what this new teaching with authority was, since even evil spirits obeyed him. It shows the reader that Jesus' power is unlike anything people had seen.
entries.1:28: News about Jesus spread quickly throughout the whole region of Galilee. It tells the reader that Jesus' impact could not be kept quiet.
entries.1:29: Leaving the synagogue, Jesus and his followers went to the home of Simon and Andrew, along with James and John. It shows the reader that Jesus' ministry happened in homes as well as public places.
entries.1:30: Simon's mother-in-law was in bed with a fever, and they told Jesus about her. It tells the reader that bringing someone's need to Jesus is the right response.
entries.1:31: Jesus took her by the hand, lifted her up, and the fever left; she then served them. It shows the reader that Jesus heals personally and that healing leads to grateful service.
entries.1:32: At sunset, people brought to Jesus all who were sick and all who were troubled by evil spirits. It tells the reader that Jesus welcomed the needy crowds, not just a select few.
entries.1:33: The whole town gathered at the door. It shows the reader how deeply people hungered for what Jesus offered.
entries.1:34: Jesus healed many with various diseases and cast out many evil spirits, but he would not let the spirits speak because they knew who he was. It tells the reader that Jesus cared for all kinds of suffering while controlling how his identity was revealed.
entries.1:35: Very early, long before daylight, Jesus got up, went to a lonely place, and prayed. It shows the reader that even Jesus needed quiet time with God, and so do we.
entries.1:36: Simon and his companions went out looking for Jesus. It tells the reader that people wanted Jesus' presence and attention.
entries.1:37: When they found him, they told him that everyone was looking for him. It shows the reader the pull of popularity and the pressure to stay where the crowds are.
entries.1:38: Jesus said they should go on to nearby towns so he could preach there too, because that was why he had come. It tells the reader that Jesus kept his mission first, not just his popularity.
entries.1:39: Jesus traveled through Galilee, preaching in the synagogues and driving out evil spirits. It shows the reader that his work combined teaching and real deliverance.
entries.1:40: A man with leprosy knelt before Jesus and said that if Jesus was willing, he could make him clean. It tells the reader that coming to Jesus with humble, honest need is the right move.
entries.1:41: Jesus felt deep compassion for the man and chose to heal him, showing that he cares about people who are suffering. You can bring your needs to a God who is moved by pity, not annoyed by them.
entries.1:42: The healing happened immediately and completely, just as Jesus said. It shows that Jesus' word has real power to change a person's condition.
entries.1:43: Jesus sent the man away with a strong, urgent warning. He had a purpose for the man's next steps and didn't want him to act on his own impulse.
entries.1:44: Jesus told him to keep quiet and instead follow the law by showing himself to the priest and giving the required offering. Obedience to God's instructions mattered more than spreading news, and the offering would serve as official proof of the healing.
entries.1:45: The man disobeyed and told everyone, which made it hard for Jesus to move around openly, so he stayed in lonely places while people still came to him from everywhere. Good news spread, but the man's failure to listen made Jesus' work harder.
entries.2:1: Jesus came back to Capernaum, and word spread quickly that he was staying in a certain house. People today can expect that news about Jesus still draws attention wherever it is shared.
entries.2:2: So many people crowded in to hear him that there was no room left, even at the door, and he taught them. When people are hungry for God's word, it is worth making the effort to hear it.
entries.2:3: Four men brought a paralyzed man to Jesus, carrying him on a mat because he could not move himself. Friends who bring someone helpless to Jesus are doing something truly valuable.
entries.2:4: They could not get through the crowd, so they dug through the roof above Jesus and lowered the man down on his mat. Determined faith will find a way to bring people to Jesus, even when obstacles are in the way.
entries.2:5: Jesus saw the faith of the men and told the paralyzed man that his sins were forgiven. Jesus cares about a person's deepest need, not just their physical problems.
entries.2:6: Some religious teachers were sitting there, quietly thinking their own thoughts about what Jesus had said. It is possible to be near Jesus and still be critical in your heart rather than open.
entries.2:7: They thought Jesus was speaking disrespectfully of God, since only God can forgive sins. Their reasoning was right about God, but they failed to see who Jesus really was.
entries.2:8: Jesus knew what they were thinking and asked them why they were arguing inwardly. Nothing in our hearts is hidden from Jesus.
entries.2:9: Jesus asked which is easier to say: that sins are forgiven, or that a paralyzed man should get up and walk. Words are easy, but Jesus was about to show real power behind his words.
entries.2:10: Jesus said this to show that he, the Son of Man, has real authority on earth to forgive sins. Forgiveness is not just a nice sentiment; it comes from Jesus' genuine authority.
entries.2:11: Jesus told the paralyzed man to get up, pick up his mat, and go home. His word carries power to change a person's whole situation.
entries.2:12: The man got up at once, took his mat, and walked out in front of everyone, and the crowd was amazed and praised God. When Jesus acts, people are left in awe and give glory to God.
entries.2:13: Jesus went out again to the lakeside, and the crowds came to him, and he taught them. Jesus kept making himself available to teach anyone who came.
entries.2:14: Jesus saw Levi, a tax collector, at his booth and simply told him to follow, and Levi got up and went. Jesus calls ordinary and even disliked people, and they can respond immediately.
entries.2:15: Jesus ate at Levi's house with many tax collectors and sinners who had begun following him. Jesus was willing to sit with people others avoided.
entries.2:16: The religious leaders asked the disciples why Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners. People who think they are respectable often question why Jesus welcomes those they look down on.
entries.2:17: Jesus said sick people need a doctor, not healthy ones, and that he came to call sinners, not the self-righteous. Jesus came for people who know they need help, not those who think they are fine.
entries.2:18: People asked Jesus why his disciples did not fast like John's disciples and the Pharisees did. It is easy to compare religious practices and miss what Jesus is actually doing.
entries.2:19: Jesus compared himself to a bridegroom and said his friends would not fast while he was still with them. There is a time to celebrate when Jesus is present, not to mourn.
entries.2:20: Jesus said the time would come when he would be taken away, and then his followers would fast. Jesus was honest that hard days were coming for his disciples.
entries.2:21: Jesus said no one patches an old coat with new cloth, because the patch would pull away and make the tear worse. His new way could not simply be patched onto the old religious system.
entries.2:22: Jesus said new wine must go into new wineskins, or both would be ruined. What Jesus brings requires a fresh response, not just an old container.
entries.2:23: On the Sabbath, as Jesus and his disciples walked through grain fields, the disciples picked heads of grain to eat. Ordinary hunger and simple actions became a point of conflict.
entries.2:24: The Pharisees challenged Jesus, saying his disciples were doing what was not allowed on the Sabbath. Religious people can turn good rules into tools for accusing others.
entries.2:25: Jesus reminded them of what David did when he and his companions were hungry. Jesus pointed to Scripture to show that human need matters in how rules are applied.
entries.2:26: Jesus recalled how David entered God's house and ate the sacred bread that only priests were allowed to eat, and shared it with his men. Even in the Old Testament, mercy for the hungry mattered.
entries.2:27: Jesus said the Sabbath was made for people's benefit, not people for the Sabbath. God's rules are meant to help us, not to crush us.
entries.2:28: Jesus concluded that he, the Son of Man, is lord even over the Sabbath. Jesus has the final say on how God's day should be understood and kept.
entries.3:1: Jesus went back into the synagogue, where a man with a crippled hand was present. The man's need sets the scene for what Jesus is about to do.
entries.3:2: The religious leaders were watching Jesus closely, hoping to catch him healing on the Sabbath so they could accuse him. They cared more about their rules than about the suffering man.
entries.3:3: Jesus told the man to stand up in front of everyone. He was not hiding what he was about to do.
entries.3:4: Jesus asked the leaders whether it is right to do good or harm on the Sabbath, to save life or destroy it. They had no answer because their silence showed they knew he was right.
entries.3:5: Jesus was angry and grieved at their stubborn refusal to care, then healed the man's hand. His anger shows that hard hearts and indifference to suffering matter to God.
entries.3:6: The Pharisees left and immediately began plotting with the Herodians to kill Jesus. Their opposition had turned into a plan for murder.
entries.3:7: Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the lake, and a large crowd from Galilee followed him. People were drawn to him from many places.
entries.3:8: Crowds came from Jerusalem, Idumea, beyond the Jordan, and around Tyre and Sidon because they had heard what he was doing. News of his works spread widely.
entries.3:9: Jesus asked his disciples to keep a small boat ready so the crowd would not crush him. He was practical about the pressure of so many people.
entries.3:10: He had healed so many that sick people were pressing in to touch him. People were desperate for healing and reached out to him.
entries.3:11: Whenever evil spirits saw Jesus they fell down before him and cried out that he was the Son of God. Even the forces of evil recognized who he was.
entries.3:12: Jesus strictly ordered the spirits not to make him known. He did not want his identity spread by the wrong voices.
entries.3:13: Jesus went up a mountain and called to himself those he wanted, and they came to him. He chose his closest followers himself.
entries.3:14: He appointed twelve to be with him and to be sent out to preach. Being with Jesus came before being sent by him.
entries.3:15: He gave them authority to drive out evil spirits. Their mission included power over the forces of evil.
entries.3:16: Simon was given the name Peter. A new name marked a new role in Jesus' plans.
entries.3:17: James and John, the sons of Zebedee, were called Boanerges, meaning Sons of Thunder. The name suggests their strong, fiery personalities.
entries.3:18: The list continues with Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, and Simon the Zealot. These were ordinary men from varied backgrounds.
entries.3:19: The last named is Judas Iscariot, who would later betray Jesus. Even among his chosen twelve, one would turn against him.
entries.3:20: Jesus went into a house and the crowd gathered again so tightly that he and his disciples could not even eat. His ministry left little room for rest.
entries.3:21: When his family heard about this, they came to take charge of him, saying he was out of his mind. Even those closest to him misunderstood him.
entries.3:22: The scribes from Jerusalem claimed Jesus was possessed by Beelzebub and cast out demons by the prince of demons. They explained his power away as evil.
entries.3:23: Jesus answered them with a story: how can Satan drive out Satan? He pointed out the absurdity of their accusation.
entries.3:24: If a kingdom is divided against itself, it cannot stand. Internal conflict destroys any group.
entries.3:25: If a household is divided against itself, it will fall apart. Division ruins families and communities.
entries.3:26: If Satan is fighting himself, he cannot survive but will come to an end. Jesus showed that their argument made no sense.
entries.3:27: No one can rob a strong man's house without first tying him up, and then he can take the goods. Jesus was saying he had come to bind the strong enemy and free those held captive.
entries.3:28: Jesus solemnly promised that people can be forgiven all their sins and all the evil things they say. God's forgiveness is wide and real.
entries.3:29: But anyone who speaks evil against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; that guilt remains forever. Rejecting God's own Spirit is a serious and lasting matter.
entries.3:30: Jesus said this because they claimed he had an unclean spirit. They were attributing God's work to evil.
entries.3:31: Jesus' mother and brothers arrived and stood outside, asking for him. His family wanted to see him while he was surrounded by a crowd.
entries.3:32: The crowd told Jesus that his mother and brothers were outside looking for him. They expected him to go to them.
entries.3:33: Jesus asked who his mother and brothers really were. He was about to redefine family in a surprising way.
entries.3:34: Looking at those seated around him, Jesus said they were his mother and brothers. He counted those who followed him as his true family.
entries.3:35: Whoever does God's will is Jesus' brother, sister, and mother. Obeying God makes a person part of his family.
entries.4:1: Jesus was teaching beside the lake, and so many people crowded around that he sat in a boat and taught from there while the crowd stood on shore. It shows how eager people were to hear him, and that his teaching was worth going out of your way for.
entries.4:2: Jesus taught the crowd many things by telling stories, and he began by urging them to listen carefully. His lessons are worth your full attention, not just a quick hearing.
entries.4:3: Jesus starts a story about a farmer who went out to scatter seed in his field. It sets up a picture of how God's message gets spread around.
entries.4:4: Some seed fell on the hard path, and birds quickly ate it up. Some people hear God's message but lose it right away before it can take hold.
entries.4:5: Some seed landed on rocky ground with little soil, so it sprouted fast because it wasn't planted deep. Quick enthusiasm can look promising but may not last.
entries.4:6: When the sun got hot, the shallow plant dried up and died because it had no real root. A faith without deep roots can wither when things get hard.
entries.4:7: Some seed fell among thorny weeds that grew up and choked it, so it produced no fruit. Other concerns in life can crowd out God's message and keep it from making a difference.
entries.4:8: Some seed fell on good soil and grew well, producing a huge crop, far more than was planted. When God's message is received well, it can produce results beyond what you'd expect.
entries.4:9: Jesus says that anyone who can hear should really listen to what he's saying. He's asking you to pay attention, because this story has something important for you.
entries.4:10: Later, when Jesus was alone with his close followers, they asked him what the stories meant. It's fine to ask questions when you don't understand something about God.
entries.4:11: Jesus told his followers that they were being let in on the secret of God's kingdom, while outsiders only got the stories. Being close to Jesus gives you understanding that others don't have.
entries.4:12: Jesus explains that some people see and hear but never really get it, so they miss the chance to turn to God and be forgiven. It's a warning that you can be near the truth and still miss it if your heart isn't open.
entries.4:13: Jesus asks his followers how they'll understand any of his stories if they can't grasp this one. This story is a foundation, so it's worth working to understand it.
entries.4:14: Jesus explains that the seed in the story stands for God's message. Wherever that message is shared, it's like seed being planted.
entries.4:15: The seed on the path represents people who hear the message, but the Evil One immediately snatches it away. Hearing alone isn't enough; the message needs to be kept and taken to heart.
entries.4:16: The seed on rocky ground stands for people who hear the message and receive it with immediate joy. A happy first reaction is good, but it isn't the whole story.
entries.4:17: These people have no deep roots, so when trouble or hardship comes because of the message, they quickly fall away. Faith needs to be rooted deeply if it's going to survive hard times.
entries.4:18: The seed among thorns stands for another group of people who hear the message. What happens next shows why simply hearing isn't enough.
entries.4:19: Worries about life, the lure of money, and wanting other things crowd out the message so it produces nothing. Everyday anxieties and desires can quietly smother what God wants to do in you.
entries.4:20: The seed on good soil stands for people who hear the message, hold onto it, and produce a great deal of fruit. Taking God's word seriously and keeping it in your heart leads to real results.
entries.4:21: Jesus points out that nobody lights a lamp and then hides it under a bowl or a bed; they put it where it can be seen. What God gives you is meant to be shown, not hidden away.
entries.4:22: Nothing hidden will stay hidden forever, and every secret will eventually be brought into the open. Live honestly, because the truth always comes out in the end.
entries.4:23: Jesus repeats that anyone who can hear should really listen. He's making sure you don't miss what he's saying.
entries.4:24: Jesus tells them to be careful about what they listen to, because the effort you put in determines what you get back, and even more will be given. Paying close attention to good teaching pays off.
entries.4:25: Whoever has something will be given more, but whoever has nothing will lose even what little they have. Using and valuing what God gives you leads to more; neglecting it leads to loss.
entries.4:26: Jesus compares God's kingdom to a man who scatters seed in the ground. It pictures something that grows from a small beginning.
entries.4:27: The man sleeps and wakes, day after day, while the seed grows without him knowing how. God's work grows on its own, even when you can't see or explain it.
entries.4:28: The soil produces the crop by itself, first a blade, then the head, then the full grain. Growth happens step by step, and God is the one who makes it happen.
entries.4:29: Once the grain is ripe, the farmer immediately brings in the harvest. There's a right time for everything, and the harvest comes when the growth is complete.
entries.4:30: Jesus asks what comparison he can use to help people picture God's kingdom. He's about to use a simple everyday image to explain something big.
entries.4:31: God's kingdom is like a mustard seed, which is tiny when it's planted. Big things for God often start very small.
entries.4:32: Once planted, that tiny seed grows into the largest plant, with branches big enough for birds to rest in. Small beginnings with God can grow into something that blesses many others.
entries.4:33: Jesus used many stories like these to teach the crowd, giving them as much as they could take in. He met people where they were and didn't overload them.
entries.4:34: Jesus always used stories when speaking to the crowd, but explained everything privately to his disciples. He wants those who follow him closely to understand what he's saying.
entries.4:35: That evening, Jesus told his disciples to go across to the other side of the lake. It was a simple instruction that led into a serious situation.
entries.4:36: They left the crowd and took Jesus along in the boat just as he was, and other boats came too. Following Jesus doesn't mean leaving everyone else behind, but it does mean going where he leads.
entries.4:37: A fierce windstorm hit, and waves were crashing into the boat until it was nearly full of water. Even when you're with Jesus, life can suddenly become frightening.
entries.4:38: Jesus was asleep on a cushion in the back of the boat, and the disciples woke him, asking if he didn't care that they were about to die. It's easy to feel like God has forgotten you when things get scary.
entries.4:39: Jesus woke up and commanded the wind and the sea to be still, and immediately there was a great calm. He has real authority over the things that frighten you.
entries.4:40: Jesus asked them why they were so afraid and whether they still had no faith. He gently challenges fear and invites you to trust him even in the storm.
entries.4:41: The disciples were terrified because Jesus had just calmed a storm with a word, and they realized he was far more than an ordinary teacher. It means you can trust that the one you follow has real authority over the things that scare you most.
entries.5:1: Jesus and his disciples crossed the lake and arrived in a non-Jewish region. This shows Jesus going to people outside his own community.
entries.5:2: As soon as Jesus stepped out of the boat, a man controlled by an evil spirit came to meet him. Trouble met him right away, but he was ready for it.
entries.5:3: The man lived among the tombs and was so strong and wild that no one could restrain him, even with a chain. He was completely cut off from normal life.
entries.5:4: People had tried many times to tie him up with chains and iron, but he broke them every time, and no one could subdue him. His condition was beyond human control.
entries.5:5: Day and night he wandered among the tombs and hills, screaming and cutting himself with stones. He was deeply tormented and hurting himself.
entries.5:6: When he spotted Jesus in the distance, he ran to him and bowed down before him. Even a tormented man was drawn to Jesus and showed him respect.
entries.5:7: He shouted loudly, asking Jesus why he was interfering and begging him not to torture him. The evil spirit recognized Jesus as God's Son and feared his power.
entries.5:8: This explains why the spirit cried out: Jesus had already commanded it to leave the man. Jesus spoke with authority and the spirit had to respond.
entries.5:9: Jesus asked the spirit its name, and it answered "Legion," meaning there were many spirits inside the man. The man's problem was far bigger than one evil spirit.
entries.5:10: The spirits begged Jesus not to send them out of that region. They knew Jesus had power over them and were desperate to stay nearby.
entries.5:11: A large herd of pigs was feeding on the hillside nearby. This detail sets up what happens next.
entries.5:12: The evil spirits asked Jesus to send them into the pigs. Even evil spirits had to ask Jesus for permission.
entries.5:13: Jesus allowed it, and the spirits entered the pigs, which rushed down the slope into the lake and drowned, about two thousand of them. The man was freed, but the pigs were lost.
entries.5:14: The men looking after the pigs ran off and reported what happened in the town and countryside, and people came out to see for themselves. News of the event spread quickly.
entries.5:15: They found the man who had been tormented sitting calmly, dressed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. The change was so dramatic it frightened them.
entries.5:16: Those who had watched told the newcomers the whole story of what happened to the man and to the pigs. Eyewitnesses confirmed the account.
entries.5:17: The people asked Jesus to leave their region. They were more unsettled by what happened than grateful, and they wanted him gone.
entries.5:18: As Jesus got back into the boat, the healed man begged to go with him. He was grateful and wanted to stay close to the one who freed him.
entries.5:19: Jesus refused but told him to go home to his family and tell them what the Lord had done for him and how he had shown mercy. Jesus gave him a mission right where he lived.
entries.5:20: The man went and told everyone in the Decapolis region what Jesus had done for him, and people were amazed. His story became a witness to many.
entries.5:21: Jesus crossed back over the lake, and a large crowd gathered around him by the shore. People were eager to be near him.
entries.5:22: A synagogue leader named Jairus came and fell at Jesus' feet. An important religious man humbled himself before Jesus.
entries.5:23: Jairus pleaded with Jesus to come and lay hands on his dying little daughter so she would live. He was a desperate father asking for help.
entries.5:24: Jesus went with him, and a large crowd followed and pressed around him. Jesus moved toward the need despite the crowd.
entries.5:25: A woman in the crowd had been bleeding for twelve years. She had a long-standing, serious health problem.
entries.5:26: She had suffered under many doctors, spent everything she had, and only got worse. Her situation was hopeless and costly.
entries.5:27: Having heard about Jesus, she came up behind him in the crowd and touched his robe. She acted quietly, hoping for healing.
entries.5:28: She thought that if she could just touch his clothes, she would be healed. Her hope was simple and specific.
entries.5:29: Immediately her bleeding stopped, and she felt in her body that she was healed. The healing was instant and real.
entries.5:30: Jesus immediately knew that power had gone out from him, so he turned and asked who had touched his robe. He noticed the healing and wanted to meet the person.
entries.5:31: The disciples pointed out that the crowd was pressing on him from all sides, so asking who touched him seemed odd. They didn't understand what he meant.
entries.5:32: Jesus kept looking around to see who had done it. He was determined to find the person who had been healed.
entries.5:33: The woman, trembling with fear and knowing what had happened, came and fell before him and told him the whole truth. She was honest about what she had done.
entries.5:34: Jesus called her "Daughter," said her faith had healed her, and told her to go in peace, free from her disease. He affirmed her and gave her peace and wholeness.
entries.5:35: While Jesus was still speaking, people came from Jairus' house saying his daughter had died and there was no point troubling Jesus further. The situation seemed hopeless.
entries.5:36: Jesus ignored what they said and told Jairus not to be afraid but to keep believing. He called for faith in the face of bad news.
entries.5:37: Jesus allowed only Peter, James, and John to go with him. He kept the group small for this particular moment.
entries.5:38: At Jairus' house, Jesus saw a commotion with people weeping and wailing loudly. The household was in grief and chaos.
entries.5:39: Jesus asked why they were making such a noise, saying the child was not dead but sleeping. He was saying the situation was not final.
entries.5:40: The people laughed at him, but he put them all outside, then took the child's parents and his companions into where the child was. He dismissed the mockers and went to the child.
entries.5:41: Taking the child's hand, Jesus told her to get up, and she immediately stood and walked, since she was twelve. He raised her with a simple command.
entries.5:42: The parents were completely amazed, and Jesus told them strictly not to tell anyone, and to give the girl something to eat. He cared for her practical needs and kept the miracle quiet.
entries.5:43: Jesus gave strict orders that no one should know about it and told them to give her something to eat. He cared for her practical needs and kept the miracle quiet.
entries.6:1: Jesus left the place where he had been and went back to his hometown, and his followers went with him. It shows that even Jesus returned to familiar places, and his disciples stayed close to him.
entries.6:2: On the Sabbath Jesus taught in the local synagogue, and people were amazed and puzzled about where he got such wisdom and power. It means people can be surprised by God's work through someone they thought they knew.
entries.6:3: The people recognized Jesus as the local carpenter, the son of Mary, with brothers and sisters they knew, and they took offense at him. It means familiarity can make people dismiss someone, and we should be careful not to reject truth because of a person's background.
entries.6:4: Jesus said a prophet is honored everywhere except in his own hometown, among his relatives, and in his own family. It means the people closest to us may be the hardest to convince, and that can be painful.
entries.6:5: Jesus could not do many mighty works there, except healing a few sick people by laying hands on them. It means unbelief can block what God might do, so our openness to him matters.
entries.6:6: Jesus was amazed at their lack of faith, and he went around the surrounding villages teaching. It means Jesus notices when people don't trust him, and he keeps teaching anyway.
entries.6:7: Jesus called the twelve disciples and sent them out in pairs, giving them authority over evil spirits. It means Jesus sends ordinary people out with real authority, and working in pairs gives support.
entries.6:8: He told them to take nothing for the trip except a walking stick—no bread, no bag, no money. It means they were to travel simply and trust God to provide through others.
entries.6:9: They were to wear ordinary sandals and not take an extra coat. It means keep it simple and don't load yourself down with extras; trust God for what you need.
entries.6:10: Jesus said wherever they entered a house, they should stay there until they left that place. It means accept hospitality and don't keep moving around looking for something better.
entries.6:11: If a place refused to welcome or listen to them, they were to shake off the dust from their feet as a warning. It means don't force your message on people who reject it; leave it with God and move on.
entries.6:12: The disciples went out preaching that people needed to change their hearts and turn from wrong. It means the core message is a real change of heart, not just outward religion.
entries.6:13: They drove out many evil spirits and healed many sick people by putting oil on them. It means Jesus' authority worked through his followers to bring freedom and healing.
entries.6:14: King Herod heard about Jesus because everyone was talking about him, and he thought John the Baptist had risen from the dead. It means guilt and fear can make people misinterpret what God is doing.
entries.6:15: Some people said Jesus was Elijah, and others said he was a prophet like the old prophets. It means people were trying to fit Jesus into familiar categories instead of seeing who he really was.
entries.6:16: When Herod heard about it, he insisted that John, whom he had killed, had come back to life. It means a guilty conscience can haunt a person and distort the truth.
entries.6:17: Herod had arrested John and put him in prison because of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, whom Herod had married. It means powerful people often silence those who confront their wrong doing.
entries.6:18: John told Herod plainly that it was wrong for him to have his brother's wife. It means speaking the truth to powerful people is right, even when it is costly.
entries.6:19: Herodias held a grudge against John and wanted to kill him, but she couldn't yet. It means resentment can grow into a desire for revenge when someone exposes our sin.
entries.6:20: Herod feared John because he knew he was a good and holy man, so he protected him; hearing him troubled Herod, yet he listened gladly. It means even a conflicted person can be drawn to truth, and God can protect his messengers for a time.
entries.6:21: The opportunity came on Herod's birthday when he gave a banquet for his officials, military captains, and leading men of Galilee. It means a festive occasion became the setting for a terrible deed.
entries.6:22: Herodias' daughter came in and danced, pleasing Herod and his guests, and the king promised to give her anything she asked. It means a rash promise made in front of others can lead to evil.
entries.6:23: He swore an oath to give her whatever she wanted, even up to half his kingdom. It means careless vows can trap us into doing things we later regret.
entries.6:24: The girl asked her mother what to request, and her mother said, the head of John the Baptist. It means a bitter heart can use even a child to carry out revenge.
entries.6:25: The girl hurried back to the king and asked for John the Baptist's head on a plate right away. It means hatred can be cold and immediate, showing how far resentment can go.
entries.6:26: The king was very sorry, but because of his oath and his guests he wouldn't refuse her. It means fear of looking bad before others can make us do wrong even when we know better.
entries.6:27: The king immediately sent an executioner with orders to bring back John's head, and he went and beheaded John in prison. It means a good man can be killed because of someone else's pride and anger.
entries.6:28: The executioner brought John's head on a plate and gave it to the girl, and she gave it to her mother. It means the revenge was completed, and the mother got what her bitterness wanted.
entries.6:29: When John's disciples heard about it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb. It means even in tragedy, faithful people honor the dead and do what is right.
entries.6:30: The twelve disciples gathered back with Jesus and reported everything they had done and taught. It means Jesus wants his followers to come back to him and share what happened.
entries.6:31: Jesus told them to come away by themselves to a quiet place and rest, because so many people were coming and going that they didn't even have time to eat. It means rest is important, and Jesus cares about our weariness.
entries.6:32: They went away in a boat to a lonely place by themselves. It means sometimes we need to step away from the crowd to be with Jesus and recover.
entries.6:33: People saw them leaving and recognized them, and many ran on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. It means people are hungry for Jesus and will go to great lengths to find him.
entries.6:34: When Jesus got out and saw the large crowd, he felt compassion for them because they were like sheep without a shepherd, and he taught them many things. It means Jesus cares about people's confusion and feeds them with truth.
entries.6:35: Late in the day, his disciples came and pointed out that the place was remote and it was already late. It means practical needs don't go away, and we should bring them to Jesus.
entries.6:36: The disciples suggested sending the crowd away to nearby farms and villages to buy food for themselves. It means their first instinct was to solve the problem by scattering people, not by trusting Jesus.
entries.6:37: Jesus told them to feed the crowd themselves, and they asked if they should spend two hundred denarii on bread for them. It means Jesus pushes us past what seems possible and asks us to bring what we have.
entries.6:38: Jesus asked how many loaves they had and told them to go check; they found five loaves and two fish. It means Jesus starts with what is already in our hands, however small.
entries.6:39: Jesus told the people to sit down in groups on the green grass. It means he organizes people with care, bringing order to a chaotic crowd.
entries.6:40: The people sat down in groups of hundreds and fifties. It means Jesus arranged them so everyone could be seen and served, showing practical care for each person.
entries.6:41: Jesus thanked God for the small amount of food, then had his disciples hand it out to the crowd. It shows that what seems far too little can become enough when it is given to God.
entries.6:42: Everyone in the crowd ate until they were full. The point is that Jesus truly met their need, not just barely but completely.
entries.6:43: The leftovers filled twelve baskets, far more than they started with. This shows the abundance of what Jesus provides.
entries.6:44: About five thousand men ate the bread, not counting women and children. The size of the crowd makes the miracle even more striking.
entries.6:45: Jesus quickly sent his disciples off in the boat toward Bethsaida while he stayed behind to dismiss the crowd. He was taking charge of the situation and making space for what came next.
entries.6:46: Once the crowd had gone, Jesus went up a mountain alone to pray. Even after a busy, demanding day, he made time to be with God.
entries.6:47: By evening the boat was out in the middle of the lake while Jesus was alone on shore. The disciples were separated from him, but he had not lost track of them.
entries.6:48: Jesus saw the disciples struggling against a headwind and came to them walking on the water, late in the night. He noticed their difficulty and moved toward them, even though it looked like he might pass by.
entries.6:49: When the disciples saw Jesus walking on the water, they thought he was a ghost and screamed. Fear made them misread what was really happening.
entries.6:50: They were terrified because they all saw him. Jesus immediately calmed them, telling them to take courage because it was really him and they had nothing to fear.
entries.6:51: Jesus got into the boat with them and the wind stopped, leaving them utterly amazed. His presence brought both calm and wonder.
entries.6:52: They still didn't understand what the feeding had shown about who Jesus was, because their minds were slow to take it in. Even after a miracle, understanding can take time.
entries.6:53: They finished crossing the lake and brought the boat to shore at Gennesaret. The journey ended safely, as Jesus had intended.
entries.6:54: As soon as they got out of the boat, people recognized Jesus. News about him spread fast wherever he went.
entries.6:55: People ran through the whole region, carrying the sick on mats to wherever they heard Jesus was. Their urgency shows how much they hoped he could help.
entries.6:56: Wherever Jesus went, people laid the sick in public places and begged just to touch the edge of his cloak, and everyone who touched it was healed. Even a small point of contact with Jesus brought wholeness.
entries.7:1: Religious leaders from Jerusalem came to watch Jesus. It shows that people in power often show up to test and challenge those who teach something new.
entries.7:2: They noticed Jesus' followers ate without doing the special hand-washing ritual. To these leaders, that looked like breaking the rules.
entries.7:3: The Pharisees and many Jews followed an old tradition of carefully washing their hands before eating. This was a custom passed down, not a command from God's law.
entries.7:4: They also washed after being in public places and washed their dishes in special ways. These were extra traditions they treated as required.
entries.7:5: The leaders asked Jesus why his followers ignored these handed-down rules. They were measuring his disciples by their traditions rather than by God's actual commands.
entries.7:6: Jesus quotes Isaiah to say these people honor God with their words while their hearts are far from him. It warns that outward religion can hide an empty heart.
entries.7:7: Their worship is pointless because they teach human rules as if they were God's commands. It's a warning not to confuse our own traditions with what God actually asks.
entries.7:8: Jesus says they set aside God's law to hold on to their own traditions. We can be guilty of the same thing when our customs crowd out what God really wants.
entries.7:9: He points out that they deliberately sidestep God's command to keep their own handed-down rules. It shows how easy it is to protect our preferences at God's expense.
entries.7:10: God's law said to honor your father and mother and to punish anyone who curses them. This is the clear command Jesus compares their tradition against.
entries.7:11: They taught that if a man declared his money 'Corban' (dedicated to God), he could keep it from helping his parents. Their rule gave him a religious excuse to neglect his family.
entries.7:12: By that rule they stopped a man from doing anything for his father or mother. A human tradition was being used to cancel a clear duty God had commanded.
entries.7:13: Their own rules made God's word ineffective, and Jesus says they do many other things like this. It's a caution that religious customs must never override what God has said.
entries.7:14: Jesus calls the crowd to listen carefully to what he is about to say. He wants everyone, not just the experts, to understand this important point.
entries.7:15: Nothing you eat or touch from outside makes you truly unclean; it's what comes out of you that does. Jesus shifts the focus from rituals to the condition of the heart.
entries.7:16: Jesus is urging anyone willing to listen to really take in what he just taught about what truly makes a person clean or unclean. It's a nudge for the reader to pay close attention and let his words actually shape how they live.
entries.7:17: When they were alone, the disciples asked Jesus to explain what he meant. It's fine to ask questions when we don't understand his teaching.
entries.7:18: Jesus gently asks if they still don't get it, then repeats that what enters a person from outside can't make them unclean. He's helping them see that uncleanness is a heart issue, not a food issue.
entries.7:19: Food just goes into the stomach and passes out of the body; it never touches the heart. Mark notes that by this Jesus declared all foods clean.
entries.7:20: Jesus says it's what comes out of a person that makes them unclean. The real source of wrong is inside us, not on our hands or plates.
entries.7:21: Evil thoughts and immoral desires come from inside, from the human heart. This means the problem is deeper than behavior; it starts within us.
entries.7:22: He lists sins like theft, murder, adultery, greed, deceit, envy, slander, pride, and foolishness. These all spring from the heart, showing how much we need inner change.
entries.7:23: All these evil things come from inside and make a person unclean. Jesus makes clear that cleansing the heart matters far more than washing hands.
entries.7:24: Jesus traveled to the region of Tyre and Sidon and tried to stay unnoticed in a house. Even so, people found out he was there.
entries.7:25: A woman whose young daughter was troubled by an evil spirit heard about him and came and fell at his feet. Her love for her child drove her to seek help.
entries.7:26: She was a Greek, a Syro-Phoenician by birth, and she begged Jesus to cast the evil spirit out of her daughter. She came as an outsider with a desperate request.
entries.7:27: Jesus said the children should be fed first, since it isn't right to take their bread and throw it to the dogs. He was testing her faith with a hard saying about Israel first.
entries.7:28: She answered that even the dogs under the table eat the crumbs the children drop. She humbly accepted his words and still trusted there was help for her.
entries.7:29: Jesus honored her answer and told her to go home because the evil spirit had left her daughter. Her persistent, humble faith was rewarded.
entries.7:30: She went home and found her child lying on the bed with the evil spirit gone. What Jesus said had already happened, even at a distance.
entries.7:31: Jesus left Tyre and traveled through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the region of Decapolis. He kept moving through Gentile territory, bringing his message beyond Israel.
entries.7:32: People brought him a man who was deaf and had trouble speaking, asking Jesus to lay his hands on him. They wanted healing for someone who couldn't ask for himself.
entries.7:33: Jesus took the man aside privately, put his fingers in his ears, and touched his tongue with spit. He used physical signs the man could feel to communicate what he was doing.
entries.7:34: Looking up to heaven, Jesus sighed deeply and said 'Ephphatha,' which means 'Be open.' His sigh shows compassion, and his word shows his authority to heal.
entries.7:35: The man's ears opened, his tongue was freed, and he could speak clearly. The healing was complete and immediate.
entries.7:36: Jesus told them not to tell anyone, but the more he asked, the more they spread the news. People couldn't keep quiet about something so amazing.
entries.7:37: The crowd was utterly amazed, saying he does everything well, even making the deaf hear and the mute speak. Their reaction points to who Jesus really is.
entries.8:1: A large crowd had gathered around Jesus and they had nothing to eat. He called his disciples over to talk about the problem.
entries.8:2: Jesus felt deep compassion for the crowd because they had stayed with him for three days and had run out of food.
entries.8:3: Jesus worried that if he sent the people home hungry, they would collapse on the way, and some had traveled a long distance.
entries.8:4: The disciples wondered how anyone could possibly find enough bread to feed such a crowd in a remote, empty place.
entries.8:5: Jesus asked them how much food they actually had, and they told him they had seven loaves of bread.
entries.8:6: Jesus told the crowd to sit down on the ground, then he gave thanks, broke the bread, and had the disciples hand it out to everyone.
entries.8:7: They also had a few small fish, and Jesus blessed them and had those passed out to the crowd too.
entries.8:8: Everyone ate and was satisfied, and the disciples collected seven baskets of leftover pieces.
entries.8:9: About four thousand people were there, and Jesus sent them home.
entries.8:10: Right after that, Jesus got into a boat with his disciples and traveled to the region of Dalmanutha.
entries.8:11: Some Pharisees came and argued with Jesus, demanding that he show them a miraculous sign from heaven to test him.
entries.8:12: Jesus was deeply grieved and refused, saying no sign would be given to that generation.
entries.8:13: Jesus left them, got back into the boat, and crossed to the other side of the lake.
entries.8:14: The disciples had forgotten to bring enough bread and had only one loaf with them in the boat.
entries.8:15: Jesus warned them to be on guard against the corrupting influence of the Pharisees and of Herod.
entries.8:16: The disciples misunderstood and started talking among themselves about having no bread.
entries.8:17: Jesus knew what they were saying and asked why they were fussing about bread, and why they still didn't understand or grasp what he had done.
entries.8:18: Jesus asked them why they had eyes but didn't see, ears but didn't hear, and why they had forgotten what he had done.
entries.8:19: Jesus reminded them that when he fed five thousand people with five loaves, they collected twelve baskets of leftovers.
entries.8:20: He then reminded them that when he fed four thousand with seven loaves, they collected seven baskets of leftovers.
entries.8:21: Jesus asked them again why they still didn't understand what all this meant.
entries.8:22: When they arrived at Bethsaida, some people brought a blind man to Jesus and begged him to touch and heal him.
entries.8:23: Jesus took the blind man by the hand and led him outside the town, then spit on his eyes, laid his hands on him, and asked if he could see anything.
entries.8:24: The man looked up and said he could see people, but they looked blurry, like walking trees.
entries.8:25: Jesus put his hands on the man's eyes again, and this time the man's sight was fully restored and he could see everything clearly.
entries.8:26: Jesus sent the man home and told him not to go back into the town.
entries.8:27: Jesus and his disciples traveled through the villages near Caesarea Philippi, and along the way he asked them who people were saying he was.
entries.8:28: The disciples answered that some people thought he was John the Baptist, others thought Elijah, and still others thought one of the prophets.
entries.8:29: Jesus then asked them directly who they thought he was, and Peter answered that he was the Christ, the promised Savior.
entries.8:30: Jesus strictly warned them not to tell anyone that he was the Christ.
entries.8:31: Jesus began teaching them that he, the Son of Man, must suffer greatly, be rejected by the religious leaders, be killed, and rise again after three days.
entries.8:32: Jesus said all this plainly, and Peter took him aside and began to argue with him about it.
entries.8:33: Jesus turned around, looked at his disciples, and sharply rebuked Peter, saying he was thinking like Satan and focused on human concerns rather than God's.
entries.8:34: Jesus called the crowd and his disciples together and said that anyone who wants to follow him must deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow him.
entries.8:35: Jesus said that whoever tries to hold on to their life will lose it, but whoever gives up their life for him and the good news will truly keep it.
entries.8:36: Jesus asked what good it does a person to gain the whole world but lose their own soul.
entries.8:37: Jesus asked what a person could possibly give in exchange for their soul.
entries.8:38: Jesus warned that whoever is ashamed of him and his words in this wicked generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of them when he comes in his Father's glory with the holy angels.
entries.9:1: Jesus told his followers that some standing there would still be alive when they saw God's kingdom arrive with power. It reminds readers that God's rule becomes visible in real history, not just in the distant future.
entries.9:2: Six days later Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain alone, and his appearance changed before their eyes. The reader is meant to see that Jesus' true glory was briefly shown to these three men.
entries.9:3: His clothes turned dazzling white, whiter than any laundry on earth could make them. This signals something heavenly and beyond ordinary human experience.
entries.9:4: Elijah and Moses appeared and were talking with Jesus. This shows Jesus standing in line with God's greatest past figures, yet as the center of the scene.
entries.9:5: Peter, not knowing what to say, offered to build three shelters for Jesus, Moses, and Elijah. It shows how easily we respond to holy moments with busy plans instead of simply listening.
entries.9:6: Peter spoke out of confusion because the three disciples were terrified. It's a honest picture of how fear can make us say things we don't fully understand.
entries.9:7: A cloud covered them and God's voice said Jesus is his beloved Son and should be listened to. The reader is being told plainly that Jesus' words carry God's own authority.
entries.9:8: When they looked around, Moses and Elijah were gone and only Jesus was there. The point is that Jesus alone remains as the one to follow.
entries.9:9: As they came down, Jesus told them to keep quiet about what they saw until he had risen from the dead. He was controlling the timing of the news so people would understand it in light of his death and resurrection.
entries.9:10: They kept the matter to themselves but argued about what rising from the dead meant. Even close followers of Jesus often didn't understand what he was saying at the time.
entries.9:11: They asked Jesus why the teachers of the law said Elijah must come first. They were trying to fit what they had just seen into the official teaching they had heard.
entries.9:12: Jesus agreed Elijah comes first to set things right, but then asked why the Scriptures say the Son of Man must suffer and be treated as nothing. He was showing that suffering was always part of God's plan, not a failure.
entries.9:13: Jesus said Elijah had already come and people treated him however they wanted, just as the Scriptures said. He was hinting that John the Baptist was that Elijah figure, and that rejection was already happening.
entries.9:14: When they returned to the other disciples, a large crowd was around them and teachers of the law were arguing with them. It shows that trouble was waiting at the bottom of the mountain while Jesus was away.
entries.9:15: As soon as the crowd saw Jesus, they were amazed and ran to greet him with respect. People were drawn to him even before he said a word.
entries.9:16: Jesus asked the crowd what they were arguing about with his disciples. He stepped straight into the conflict rather than avoiding it.
entries.9:17: A man in the crowd said he had brought his son, who was controlled by a spirit that kept him from speaking. He was desperate and looking for help from Jesus.
entries.9:18: The spirit threw the boy into fits, made him foam and grind his teeth, and left him weak, and the disciples could not cast it out. The father's helplessness shows how limited human effort is without real faith.
entries.9:19: Jesus expressed frustration at a faithless generation and asked how long he would have to put up with them, then told them to bring the boy. His words show that lack of faith is a real problem, not just a minor weakness.
entries.9:20: When the boy was brought, the spirit immediately threw him into a violent fit on the ground. The evil was real and aggressive, not something imaginary.
entries.9:21: Jesus asked the father how long the boy had been like this, and the father said since childhood. Jesus was drawing out the depth of the family's long suffering.
entries.9:22: The father said the spirit often threw the boy into fire and water to destroy him, then begged Jesus to help if he could. He was honest about his fear and his hope at the same time.
entries.9:23: Jesus picked up on the father's 'if you can' and said everything is possible for the one who believes. He was turning the focus from his own power to the father's faith.
entries.9:24: The father cried out that he did believe and asked Jesus to help his weak faith. This is one of the most honest prayers in the Bible, admitting both faith and doubt together.
entries.9:25: Seeing the crowd running up, Jesus commanded the deaf and mute spirit to come out of the boy and never return. He acted with authority and also with concern about the growing commotion.
entries.9:26: The spirit screamed, shook the boy violently, and came out, leaving him looking dead so that many said he was dead. The healing looked like a disaster before it looked like a rescue.
entries.9:27: Jesus took the boy by the hand, lifted him up, and he stood. Jesus didn't just remove the evil; he personally restored the boy.
entries.9:28: Later, privately, the disciples asked Jesus why they couldn't drive the spirit out. They wanted to understand their failure, which is a healthy response.
entries.9:29: Jesus said this kind only comes out through prayer. Some spiritual battles are not won by technique or confidence but by dependence on God.
entries.9:30: They traveled through Galilee, and Jesus wanted no one to know where they were. He was deliberately making space to teach his disciples privately.
entries.9:31: Jesus told them he would be handed over to men, killed, and rise again after three days. He was preparing them ahead of time so his death would not catch them completely off guard.
entries.9:32: The disciples didn't understand what he meant and were afraid to ask him. Fear often keeps people from asking the very questions they most need answered.
entries.9:33: When they reached Capernaum and were inside the house, Jesus asked what they had been arguing about on the road. He knew and was inviting them to be honest.
entries.9:34: They stayed silent because they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest. It's a familiar human embarrassment: we know our ambitions are small when someone asks us directly.
entries.9:35: Jesus sat down, called the twelve, and said that anyone who wants to be first must be last and serve everyone. He turned the world's idea of greatness completely upside down.
entries.9:36: Jesus took a small child, placed him among them, and held him in his arms. He used a living example, not just words, to make his point.
entries.9:37: Jesus said that welcoming a little child in his name is welcoming him, and welcoming him is welcoming God who sent him. The reader is being told that how we treat the least important people is how we treat God himself.
entries.9:38: John told Jesus they had tried to stop a man casting out demons in Jesus' name because he wasn't one of their group. It shows how quickly followers of Jesus can become possessive of his power.
entries.9:39: Jesus told them not to stop him, because no one who does a mighty work in his name can turn around and speak evil of him right away. He was teaching a generous, non-tribal attitude.
entries.9:40: Jesus said whoever is not against us is for us. It's a simple rule for recognizing allies instead of treating everyone outside the group as an enemy.
entries.9:41: Even a small kindness done to someone because they belong to Christ counts, and God will not forget to reward it. Your simple acts of service matter more than they seem.
entries.9:42: Causing a young or vulnerable believer to stumble in their faith is a serious wrong, serious enough that drowning would be preferable. Be careful how your words and actions affect those who are new or weak in faith.
entries.9:43: Jesus uses strong picture language to say that anything causing you to sin should be removed, because losing it is far better than losing your life with God. Deal decisively with whatever pulls you away from him.
entries.9:44: This repeats the warning that the fire punishing sin never goes out, showing how serious it is to let sin rule your life. It means you should take sin seriously now rather than treat it lightly.
entries.9:45: The same urgent point is repeated with the foot: cut off whatever leads you into sin, because entering life with less is better than being lost with everything. Take your own sin seriously enough to make hard changes.
entries.9:46: This again repeats the same warning about unending fire, stressing that the consequence of sin is real and lasting. It means you should deal with sin in your life instead of ignoring it.
entries.9:47: The eye is another example: remove what causes you to sin, because entering God's kingdom with less is better than being thrown away with everything. Let nothing be too precious to give up for God.
entries.9:48: This pictures a place of unending ruin, where decay and fire never stop. It is a sober warning that rejecting God has permanent consequences.
entries.9:49: Fire, like salt, is used here as a picture of testing and purification that everyone will face. Trials can refine your faith rather than destroy it.
entries.9:50: Salt is useful, but it can lose its purpose; in the same way, keep your faith real and live at peace with one another. Let your life stay distinct and peaceful toward others.
entries.10:1: Jesus traveled to a new region and, as usual, crowds gathered and he taught them. It shows that teaching people was a steady habit of his, not a one-time event.
entries.10:2: Religious leaders tried to trap Jesus with a question about whether divorce was allowed. They were testing him, not honestly seeking an answer.
entries.10:3: Jesus turned the question back on them, asking what their own law had said. He wanted them to think about the source of their practice.
entries.10:4: They answered that Moses allowed a man to divorce his wife by giving her a written notice. That was the rule they were relying on.
entries.10:5: Jesus said that rule existed only because people's hearts were stubborn and hard. It was a concession, not God's original ideal.
entries.10:6: Jesus pointed back to the beginning, when God made people male and female. He was grounding marriage in God's design, not in later rules.
entries.10:7: This means a man leaves his parents and forms a new, close bond with his wife. Marriage creates a new primary relationship.
entries.10:8: The two become so united that they count as one, not two separate people. Marriage is meant to be a deep union, not a loose arrangement.
entries.10:9: Since God joins a couple together, people should not tear that bond apart. It's a serious warning against treating marriage as disposable.
entries.10:10: Later, away from the crowd, the disciples asked Jesus more about this. They wanted to understand what he had just said.
entries.10:11: Jesus said that a man who divorces his wife and marries another is unfaithful to her. He was holding up the seriousness of the marriage bond.
entries.10:12: He applied the same standard to a woman who divorces her husband and marries another. Both are held to the same faithfulness.
entries.10:13: People brought young children for Jesus to touch and bless, but the disciples scolded them. The disciples thought children were not important enough to bother him.
entries.10:14: Jesus was upset at his disciples and insisted the children be allowed to come to him. He said God's kingdom belongs to people like them.
entries.10:15: Jesus said that unless a person receives God's kingdom like a child does, they won't enter it. It means coming to God with simple trust, not self-importance.
entries.10:16: Jesus held the children and blessed them with his hands. He showed real warmth and care toward them.
entries.10:17: A man ran up, knelt before Jesus, and asked what he must do to have eternal life. He was earnest and respectful, wanting to know how to be right with God.
entries.10:18: Jesus challenged the man's use of the word good, saying only God is truly good. He was nudging him to think about who he was really talking to.
entries.10:19: Jesus listed several of God's commands about how to treat others, like not murdering, stealing, or lying. He pointed the man to the moral law he already knew.
entries.10:20: The man said he had kept all these commands since he was young. He believed he had done what was required.
entries.10:21: Jesus looked at him with love and told him to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and follow him. He was asking for the one thing the man was not willing to give up.
entries.10:22: The man's face fell and he walked away sad because he owned a lot of property. His wealth kept him from following Jesus.
entries.10:23: Jesus looked around and told his disciples how hard it is for rich people to enter God's kingdom. Wealth can make people feel self-sufficient and hold them back.
entries.10:24: The disciples were amazed at his words, so Jesus repeated that trusting in wealth makes entering God's kingdom very hard. The danger is putting confidence in money rather than God.
entries.10:25: Jesus used a vivid picture: a camel going through a needle's eye is easier than a rich person entering God's kingdom. It sounds impossible on purpose, to show how strong the pull of wealth is.
entries.10:26: The disciples were shocked and asked who could possibly be saved then. They assumed wealth was a sign of God's favor, so this seemed to rule everyone out.
entries.10:27: Jesus said saving people is impossible for humans but not for God, because God can do all things. Salvation is God's work, not something we achieve.
entries.10:28: Peter pointed out that they had left everything to follow Jesus. He was asking, in effect, what they would get for their sacrifice.
entries.10:29: Jesus said no one who has given up home, family, or land for his sake and the good news goes unrewarded. Sacrifice for him is never ignored.
entries.10:30: He promised they would receive far more, along with troubles, in this life, and eternal life in the world to come. Following Jesus brings both blessing and hardship now, and full reward later.
entries.10:31: Jesus said many who seem first will end up last, and those who seem last will be first. God's way of ranking people is not the same as ours.
entries.10:32: As they walked toward Jerusalem, Jesus led the way while the others were amazed and afraid. He then took the twelve aside to tell them what was coming.
entries.10:33: Jesus said he would be handed over to the religious leaders, condemned to death, and given to the foreign rulers. He was openly predicting his suffering.
entries.10:34: He said they would mock him, spit on him, beat him, and kill him, but after three days he would rise again. He was telling them plainly about his death and resurrection.
entries.10:35: James and John came to Jesus and asked him to grant whatever they requested. They were angling for a favor before saying what it was.
entries.10:36: Jesus simply asked them what they wanted him to do. He invited them to state their request openly.
entries.10:37: They asked to sit at his right and left in his glory, the places of highest honor. They wanted top positions in his kingdom.
entries.10:38: Jesus said they didn't know what they were asking and asked if they could drink his cup and undergo his baptism. He meant sharing in his suffering, which they hadn't considered.
entries.10:39: They confidently said they could, and Jesus said they would indeed share his cup and baptism. They would face suffering too, though they didn't understand it yet.
entries.10:40: Jesus said granting those honored seats isn't his to give; they are for those for whom they have been prepared. The places of honor are decided by God, not handed out on request.
entries.10:41: The other ten disciples were upset with James and John for asking to be honored above everyone else. It's a warning that wanting to be more important than others causes conflict, even among friends.
entries.10:42: Jesus points out that worldly rulers use their power to boss people around. He is showing that his followers should not copy that kind of leadership.
entries.10:43: Jesus says greatness in his kingdom works the opposite way: the one who wants to be great must serve others. For the reader, real importance is measured by how you treat and help people.
entries.10:44: To be first, a person must be the servant of everyone. Jesus is calling his followers to put others ahead of themselves rather than chasing status.
entries.10:45: Jesus himself came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life to save people. His example shows that self-giving love, not power, is the heart of following him.
entries.10:46: As Jesus and a large crowd left Jericho, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus was sitting by the road asking for money. He was poor and helpless, depending on others' kindness.
entries.10:47: When Bartimaeus heard Jesus was passing by, he cried out for mercy, calling him the Son of David. He believed Jesus could help him and was not afraid to ask.
entries.10:48: The crowd told him to be quiet, but he shouted even louder for mercy. His persistence shows that we should keep calling on Jesus even when others try to discourage us.
entries.10:49: Jesus stopped and told the crowd to call the blind man. Their words changed from scolding to encouragement, showing that Jesus notices and welcomes those others push aside.
entries.10:50: The blind man threw off his coat, jumped up, and came to Jesus. His quick, eager response shows real faith that acts without hesitation.
entries.10:51: Jesus asked what he wanted, and he answered plainly that he wanted to see. Jesus invites us to bring our specific needs to him honestly.
entries.10:52: Jesus told him his faith had healed him, and he immediately could see and followed Jesus on the road. Faith in Jesus brings real change and leads a person to follow him.
entries.11:1: Jesus and his disciples are getting close to Jerusalem and stop near a couple of small villages on the Mount of Olives. He sends two of them ahead to do a quick errand for him.
entries.11:2: He tells them to go into the village ahead, where they will find a young donkey tied up that no one has ever ridden. They are to untie it and bring it back to him.
entries.11:3: If anyone asks why they are taking the donkey, they should simply say the Lord needs it and will return it soon. This shows Jesus was in charge of the plan and expected it to go smoothly.
entries.11:4: The two disciples went and found the donkey tied outside a door on the street, just as Jesus had said. They started to untie it.
entries.11:5: Some people standing there asked them what they were doing untying the donkey. It was a natural question since it wasn't their animal.
entries.11:6: The disciples gave the answer Jesus had told them to give, and the people let them take the donkey without any trouble.
entries.11:7: They brought the donkey to Jesus and put their coats on its back for him to sit on, and he rode it. This was a humble way for him to enter the city, not a grand royal entrance.
entries.11:8: Many people spread their coats on the road, and others threw down leafy branches they had cut from the fields. They were treating Jesus like an honored king arriving in town.
entries.11:9: The crowd both in front of and behind Jesus shouted praises, welcoming him as the one who comes in the Lord's name. They were openly honoring him as someone sent by God.
entries.11:10: They were cheering for the kingdom that their ancestor David had been promised, and giving glory to God in the highest. They hoped Jesus was bringing that promised kingdom to life.
entries.11:11: Jesus went into Jerusalem and looked around the Temple, but since it was already evening, he left with the twelve disciples to spend the night in Bethany. He was surveying the place before acting.
entries.11:12: The next day, as they were leaving Bethany, Jesus was hungry. This reminds us that he was a real person with ordinary human needs.
entries.11:13: He saw a fig tree with leaves from a distance and went to check for fruit, but found only leaves because it wasn't the season for figs. The tree looked promising but had nothing to offer.
entries.11:14: Jesus spoke to the tree, saying no one would ever eat fruit from it again, and his disciples heard him. This was a lesson about looking fruitful but producing nothing.
entries.11:15: When they got to Jerusalem, Jesus went into the Temple and drove out the people buying and selling there, flipping the money-changers' tables and the benches of those selling doves. He was clearing out business from a place meant for worship.
entries.11:16: He also stopped people from carrying goods through the Temple courts, treating it as a shortcut. He wanted the Temple treated as a sacred place, not a marketplace.
entries.11:17: Jesus taught them that God's house was meant to be a place of prayer for all nations, but they had turned it into a hideout for thieves. He was pointing out how far they had drifted from God's purpose.
entries.11:18: When the chief priests and teachers of the law heard about this, they started looking for a way to kill him, because they were afraid of him since the crowds were amazed at his teaching. His popularity made him a threat to them.
entries.11:19: Each evening Jesus and his disciples left the city to stay somewhere else. He didn't stay overnight in Jerusalem during this time.
entries.11:20: The next morning, as they passed by, they saw that the fig tree had withered completely, right down to its roots. What Jesus had said had fully come true.
entries.11:21: Peter remembered what had happened and pointed out to Jesus that the tree he had cursed was now dead. He was surprised at how quickly it had happened.
entries.11:22: Jesus answered them by telling them to have faith in God. He was turning their attention from the dead tree to the power that comes from trusting God.
entries.11:23: Jesus said that anyone who tells a mountain to throw itself into the sea, without doubting in their heart but believing what they say will happen, will get what they ask for. He was teaching that real faith in God is powerful.
entries.11:24: Pray expecting that God hears you. Trusting him is part of the praying.
entries.11:25: When you pray, forgive anyone you have something against, so that your Father in heaven will forgive your sins too. Holding grudges blocks the forgiveness we want from God.
entries.11:26: This verse says that if you refuse to forgive others, God will not forgive you either. It means the way you treat people who wrong you affects your own standing with God, so forgiveness is not optional.
entries.11:27: They came back to Jerusalem, and while Jesus was walking in the Temple, the chief priests, teachers of the law, and elders came up to him. These were the religious leaders challenging him.
entries.11:28: They asked Jesus what right he had to do these things, and who gave him that authority. They were questioning whether he had any legitimate permission to act as he did.
entries.11:29: Jesus said he would answer their question if they first answered one of his. He was turning the tables on them with a fair trade.
entries.11:30: He asked them whether John's baptism came from heaven or from people, and told them to answer him. This put them in a difficult spot.
entries.11:31: They discussed it among themselves, realizing that if they said John's baptism was from heaven, Jesus would ask why they didn't believe him. They were trapped by their own logic.
entries.11:32: But if they said it was merely from people, they were afraid of the crowd, since everyone believed John was a real prophet. They were more worried about public opinion than the truth.
entries.11:33: So they told Jesus they didn't know, and he replied that he wouldn't tell them by what authority he did these things either. Since they wouldn't answer honestly, he didn't owe them an answer.
entries.12:1: Jesus told a story about a landowner who built a vineyard, rented it to farmers, and left on a journey. It's a picture of God entrusting his people with something valuable and expecting them to care for it faithfully.
entries.12:2: The owner sent a servant to collect his share of the harvest. God sends messengers to his people expecting them to respond with the fruit of faithful lives.
entries.12:3: The farmers beat the servant and sent him back empty-handed. People often reject God's messengers and refuse to give him what is rightfully his.
entries.12:4: The owner sent another servant, and the farmers hurt him badly and treated him shamefully. God keeps reaching out patiently, even when people respond with cruelty.
entries.12:5: The owner sent more servants, and the farmers killed some and beat others. Rejecting God's messengers is serious, and it shows how far people can drift from God.
