entries.12:6: The owner finally sent his beloved son, hoping the farmers would respect him. God sent his own Son, expecting people to honor him above all.
entries.12:7: The farmers saw the son and decided to kill him so the property would become theirs. Greed and rebellion can lead people to reject God's own Son rather than submit to him.
entries.12:8: They killed the son and threw his body out of the vineyard. Jesus was describing his own coming death at the hands of those who should have welcomed him.
entries.12:9: The owner will come, destroy those farmers, and give the vineyard to others. God will judge those who reject his Son and entrust his work to people who will honor him.
entries.12:10: Jesus quoted a psalm about a stone the builders rejected that became the most important stone. People may reject God's chosen one, but God will make him the center of everything.
entries.12:11: This surprising reversal is the Lord's own doing and deserves our wonder. God often works in ways that overturn human expectations.
entries.12:12: The leaders wanted to arrest Jesus because they knew the story was about them, but they feared the crowd. People can recognize the truth about themselves yet resist it out of fear.
entries.12:13: They sent Pharisees and Herodians to trap Jesus with his own words. Opposition to Jesus often comes through flattery and carefully set traps.
entries.12:14: They flattered Jesus and asked whether it was right to pay taxes to Caesar. They hoped his answer would get him in trouble with either the people or the government.
entries.12:15: Jesus saw through their hypocrisy and asked for a coin to look at. He was not fooled by their smooth words and exposed their real motives.
entries.12:16: Jesus asked whose image and name were on the coin, and they answered Caesar's. The coin belonged to the ruler who made it, which set up his answer.
entries.12:17: Jesus said to give Caesar what belongs to Caesar and to God what belongs to God. We can fulfill our duties to government while giving our whole lives to God, whose image we bear.
entries.12:18: The Sadducees, who denied that the dead rise, came to question Jesus. People who reject God's truth often try to trap it with clever arguments.
entries.12:19: They cited Moses' law that a man should marry his dead brother's widow to raise children for him. This was a real practice meant to protect family lines and widows.
entries.12:20: They told of seven brothers who each married the same woman in turn. Their story was designed to make belief in resurrection look absurd.
entries.12:21: The second and third brothers also married her and died without children. The story keeps building toward their trick question.
entries.12:22: All seven brothers married her and died childless, and then the woman died too. Their setup was meant to make the resurrection seem impossible to sort out.
entries.12:23: They asked whose wife she would be in the resurrection since all seven had married her. Their question assumed that life after death would work just like life now.
entries.12:24: Jesus said their error came from not knowing the Scriptures or God's power. Many doubts about God come from misunderstanding what he has said and what he can do.
entries.12:25: Jesus explained that in the resurrection people don't marry but are like angels in heaven. Life after death is real but different from our present life, so we shouldn't measure it by earthly rules.
entries.12:26: Jesus pointed to Moses and the burning bush, where God called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God spoke of these men as still his people, showing that they were alive to him.
entries.12:27: Jesus said God is the God of the living, not the dead, so the Sadducees were badly mistaken. Those who belong to God live on with him even after death.
entries.12:28: A scribe who heard the debate and liked Jesus' answer asked him which commandment was the most important. People genuinely seeking truth can come to Jesus with honest questions.
entries.12:29: Jesus began with the core confession of Israel's faith: the Lord our God is one Lord. There is only one true God, and he deserves our undivided loyalty.
entries.12:30: Jesus said to love God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength. God wants our whole selves, not just a small part of our lives.
entries.12:31: Jesus said the second command is to love your neighbor as yourself. Loving God and loving people go together and sum up what God asks of us.
entries.12:32: The scribe agreed that Jesus was right and that there is only one God. He recognized the truth in Jesus' answer and affirmed it.
entries.12:33: The scribe said loving God and neighbor with your whole being matters more than all sacrifices. God cares more about genuine love than about religious rituals.
entries.12:34: Jesus saw the scribe's wise answer and told him he was not far from God's kingdom. Honest understanding brings a person close to God, but it still takes a step of faith to enter.
entries.12:35: While teaching in the temple, Jesus asked how the scribes could say the Messiah is David's son. He was challenging their understanding of who the Messiah really is.
entries.12:36: Jesus quoted David, who by the Holy Spirit called the Messiah his Lord and pictured him seated at God's right hand. The Messiah is greater than a mere descendant of David.
entries.12:37: Jesus pointed out that David calls him Lord, so how can he be merely his son? The Messiah is both David's descendant and David's Lord, and the crowd listened gladly.
entries.12:38: Jesus warned the people to watch out for scribes who love to wear impressive robes and be greeted with respect in public. Pride and love of attention can corrupt religious leaders.
entries.12:39: He described them taking the best seats in synagogues and the places of honor at feasts. Seeking status and recognition is a danger for anyone who claims to serve God.
entries.12:40: Jesus said they take advantage of widows and pray long prayers to look holy. God sees through outward show and will judge those who use religion to exploit others.
entries.12:41: Jesus sat near the temple offering boxes and watched people drop in their money, and many rich people gave large amounts. He was paying attention to how people gave, not just how much.
entries.12:42: A poor widow came and gave two tiny coins, worth almost nothing. Her gift was small in value but came from someone with very little.
entries.12:43: Jesus called his disciples over and told them plainly that this poor widow had given more than everyone else. He was teaching them that God measures giving differently than people do.
entries.12:44: The rich gave out of their surplus, but she gave everything she had to live on. What matters to God is how much of ourselves we give, not the size of the gift.
entries.13:1: A disciple was impressed by the size and beauty of the temple buildings and pointed them out to Jesus. It's a reminder that we can admire impressive things, but they don't last forever.
entries.13:2: Jesus told him that these grand buildings would be completely destroyed, with not one stone left on another. Even the most solid things we trust in can be torn down, so our confidence shouldn't rest in them.
entries.13:3: Jesus sat on the Mount of Olives across from the temple, and four of his closest followers asked him privately what he had meant. Close friends often bring their real questions to Jesus when no one else is listening.
entries.13:4: They wanted to know when all this would happen and what warning sign would come first. It's natural to want to know the future, but Jesus answers with how to live rather than a timetable.
entries.13:5: Jesus' first warning was to be careful not to be fooled by anyone. Staying alert against deception matters more than figuring out dates.
entries.13:6: Many will come claiming to be him or to speak for him, and they will lead people away from the truth. We should test claims against what Jesus actually said rather than follow confident-sounding voices.
entries.13:7: When you hear about wars and rumors of wars, don't panic, because these things must happen but they don't mean the end has come. Bad news is not a signal to despair.
entries.13:8: Nations and kingdoms will fight, and there will be earthquakes and famines in various places, but these are only the beginning of troubles. Hard times are real, yet they are not the final word.
entries.13:9: Jesus warned his followers they would be handed over to councils, beaten in synagogues, and brought before rulers and kings because of him, as a testimony to them. Following Jesus can cost us, but even our trials can become a witness to others.
entries.13:10: The good news must first be spread to all nations. The message about Jesus is meant for everyone, everywhere, before the end comes.
entries.13:11: When you are arrested and put on trial, don't worry ahead of time about what to say; say whatever is given to you at that moment, because the Holy Spirit will speak through you. God promises to supply the words when we need them.
entries.13:12: Brothers will betray brothers to death, fathers will hand over their children, and children will turn against their parents and cause them to be killed. Faithfulness to Jesus can divide even the closest families.
entries.13:13: You will be hated by everyone because of me, but the one who endures to the end will be saved. Being disliked for Jesus is expected, and staying faithful through it is what matters.
entries.13:14: When you see the hated thing that brings destruction standing where it should not be, those in Judea should flee to the mountains. When danger is obvious, don't stay and argue; get out and get safe.
entries.13:15: Someone on the roof shouldn't go back down into the house to grab anything. In an emergency, don't risk your life for possessions.
entries.13:16: Someone out in the field shouldn't turn back to fetch a coat. Leave what you can't carry and don't delay.
entries.13:17: It will be especially hard in those days for pregnant women and nursing mothers. Jesus is honest that terrible times hit the most vulnerable hardest.
entries.13:18: Pray that it won't happen in winter. Even in predicting hardship, Jesus invites his followers to pray about the details.
entries.13:19: Those days will bring suffering worse than anything since God made the world, and nothing like it will ever happen again. Jesus doesn't soften how severe the trouble will be.
entries.13:20: If the Lord hadn't cut those days short, no one would survive, but for the sake of his chosen people he shortened them. God limits the suffering of his people and doesn't let it run unchecked.
entries.13:21: If anyone tells you, 'Look, here is the Messiah,' or 'Look, there he is,' don't believe it. Don't chase after exciting claims about where Jesus is hiding.
entries.13:22: False messiahs and false prophets will appear and perform signs and wonders to try to deceive even God's chosen people. Miracles alone don't prove someone is from God, so we need discernment.
entries.13:23: So be on your guard; Jesus has told you everything ahead of time. Being forewarned means we shouldn't be caught off guard.
entries.13:24: After that time of trouble, the sun will go dark and the moon will stop shining. Even the fixed order of the sky will be shaken.
entries.13:25: Stars will fall from the sky, and the heavenly powers will be shaken. The whole universe will show that something enormous is happening.
entries.13:26: Then people will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory. Jesus will return visibly and unmistakably, not in secret.
entries.13:27: He will send his angels to gather his chosen people from every direction, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven. God's people will be brought together from everywhere.
entries.13:28: Learn a lesson from the fig tree: when its branches soften and leaves appear, you know summer is near. Ordinary signs help us recognize what's coming.
entries.13:29: In the same way, when you see these things happening, you can know he is near, right at the door. The signs are meant to make us ready, not to satisfy our curiosity.
entries.13:30: Jesus said plainly that this generation would not pass away before all these things happened. He staked his credibility on events his own listeners would live to see.
entries.13:31: Heaven and earth will pass away, but Jesus' words will never pass away. Everything else can fail, but what Jesus says stands forever.
entries.13:32: No one knows the day or hour, not even the angels in heaven or the Son, only the Father. Anyone who claims to know the exact date is wrong.
entries.13:33: Be careful, stay awake, and pray, because you don't know when the time will come. Since we don't know the timing, we should live ready every day.
entries.13:34: It's like a man who went on a journey, left his house in charge of his servants, gave each one their work, and told the doorkeeper to stay alert. We've each been given work to do while the master is away.
entries.13:35: So stay awake, because you don't know when the master of the house will return, whether in the evening, at midnight, at dawn, or in the morning. Readiness means staying faithful at any hour.
entries.13:36: Otherwise he might come suddenly and find you asleep. The danger isn't just missing him but being caught unprepared.
entries.13:37: What Jesus says to those disciples, he says to everyone: stay awake. This call to watchfulness is for every follower, not just the first ones.
entries.14:1: The religious leaders were secretly plotting to arrest and kill Jesus just before the Passover festival. It shows how far people will go to protect their own position, and reminds us that opposition to God's work can be calculated and quiet.
entries.14:2: They wanted to avoid a public arrest during the festival because they feared a riot among the crowds. Even evil plans are often shaped by fear of what people will think, and this shows how careful and cowardly their scheming was.
entries.14:3: A woman came to a dinner in Bethany and poured expensive perfume over Jesus' head. Her generous, costly act of devotion stands in contrast to the plotting around him, and it invites us to ask what we are willing to give him.
entries.14:4: Some of those present were annoyed and asked why such costly oil was wasted. People often measure devotion by its usefulness, but love for Jesus can look wasteful to those who don't share it.
entries.14:5: They calculated the oil was worth about a year's wages and said it could have been sold to help the poor, while also criticizing the woman. Their concern for the poor was mostly talk, and it shows how easy it is to hide selfishness behind good causes.
entries.14:6: Jesus told them to leave her alone because she had done something kind for him. He defends those who love him sincerely, even when others misunderstand or criticize them.
entries.14:7: Jesus said the poor would always be around to help, but he would not always be with them. There are ordinary opportunities to do good every day, but some moments of devotion to Jesus come only once.
entries.14:8: She did what she could, anointing his body ahead of his burial. Jesus saw her act as preparing him for death, and it shows that even small, limited acts of love are fully accepted.
entries.14:9: Jesus promised that wherever the good news is preached, this woman's act would be remembered. God notices and honors quiet devotion, and her story is part of the gospel itself.
entries.14:10: Judas, one of Jesus' twelve closest followers, went to the chief priests to arrange to hand Jesus over. Betrayal can come from those closest to us, and it warns that proximity to Jesus is not the same as loyalty to him.
entries.14:11: The leaders were delighted and promised Judas money, and he began looking for a good chance to betray Jesus. Greed and opportunity came together, showing how a heart can turn against someone it once followed.
entries.14:12: On the day the Passover lamb was killed, the disciples asked Jesus where they should prepare the meal. The timing matters because Jesus himself would soon be killed as the true Passover lamb.
entries.14:13: Jesus sent two disciples into the city and told them to follow a man carrying a water jar. He gave them clear, specific instructions, showing that he knew in advance what would happen and was in control.
entries.14:14: They were to tell the owner of the house that the Teacher needed his guest room to eat the Passover with his disciples. Jesus arranged the details himself, and the room was to be given for his use.
entries.14:15: The owner would show them a large, furnished upstairs room, and there they were to prepare the meal. God provides what is needed for fellowship with him, often more than we expect.
entries.14:16: The disciples went, found everything exactly as Jesus had said, and prepared the Passover. Their obedience confirmed his words, and it encourages us to trust and act on what he tells us.
entries.14:17: When evening came, Jesus arrived with the twelve disciples. He chose to spend this last evening with his closest followers, even knowing one would betray him.
entries.14:18: While they were eating, Jesus said plainly that one of them, someone sharing his meal, would betray him. He did not hide the painful truth, and it shows that betrayal hurts most when it comes from a friend at the table.
entries.14:19: The disciples were deeply grieved and each asked whether it was him. Their reaction shows honest self-examination, and it invites us to ask the same question about our own loyalty.
entries.14:20: Jesus identified the betrayer as one of the twelve, someone dipping bread into the same dish with him. The betrayal was personal and close, not the act of an outsider.
entries.14:21: Jesus said he would go to his death as the Scriptures foretold, but great sorrow awaits the one who betrays him. God's plan will be fulfilled, yet the person who chooses to betray him is still responsible and will suffer for it.
entries.14:22: During the meal Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying it was his body. He was showing that his death would be given for them, and he invites his followers to receive him.
entries.14:23: Jesus took a cup, gave thanks, and passed it to them, and they all drank from it. The shared cup shows that his coming death was for all of them together, not just for one.
entries.14:24: Jesus said the cup was his blood of the covenant, poured out for many. He was explaining that his death would establish a new relationship between God and people.
entries.14:25: Jesus promised he would not drink wine again until he drank it new in God's kingdom. It points forward to a future celebration with his people, giving hope beyond his death.
entries.14:26: After singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. Even on the night before his suffering, Jesus worshiped with his disciples, and worship was part of his last hours with them.
entries.14:27: Jesus told them they would all abandon him that night, as Scripture said the shepherd would be struck and the sheep scattered. He warned them honestly so they would not be caught off guard.
entries.14:28: Jesus promised that after rising from the dead he would go ahead of them to Galilee. Even in the middle of failure, he gave them hope of being gathered back together.
entries.14:29: Peter insisted that even if everyone else abandoned Jesus, he would not. His confidence was sincere but too sure of himself, and it warns us against trusting our own strength.
entries.14:30: Jesus told Peter that before the rooster crowed twice that very night, he would deny knowing him three times. Jesus knew Peter's weakness better than Peter did, yet he still loved and warned him.
entries.14:31: Peter insisted he would never deny Jesus, even if it meant dying with him, and all the others said the same. Their devotion was real, but good intentions alone cannot carry us through testing.
entries.14:32: They came to a place called Gethsemane, and Jesus told his disciples to sit while he prayed. Even Jesus turned to prayer in a time of deep distress, showing where to go when we are overwhelmed.
entries.14:33: Jesus took Peter, James, and John with him and was filled with grief and deep distress. He let his closest friends near in his hardest moment, showing that even he needed companionship.
entries.14:34: Jesus told them his soul was deeply sorrowful, almost to death, and asked them to stay and watch with him. He was honest about his pain and asked for support rather than hiding it.
entries.14:35: He went a little farther, fell to the ground, and prayed that if possible the hour might pass from him. He faced real anguish and brought it honestly to God.
entries.14:36: Jesus called God his Father and asked him to take away the cup of suffering, yet chose God's will over his own. He shows us that honest prayer can include wanting another way while still submitting to God.
entries.14:37: Jesus came back and found them sleeping, and asked Peter whether he could not stay awake even one hour. The one who had just promised to be loyal was asleep, showing how quickly good intentions fade.
entries.14:38: Jesus told them to watch and pray so they would not fall into temptation, because the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak. Prayer is our protection in times of testing, since our own strength is not enough.
entries.14:39: Jesus went away again and prayed the same words. He kept bringing the same request to God, showing that persistent, repeated prayer is not wrong.
entries.14:40: He came back and found them sleeping again because their eyes were heavy, and they did not know what to say. Their failure left them speechless, a reminder of how weak we are without God's help.
entries.14:41: Jesus came a third time and told them to sleep on and take their rest, since the hour had come and he was about to be handed over. The time for watching was over, and events were now moving quickly toward his arrest.
entries.14:42: Jesus knows his betrayer is arriving and tells his friends to get up and face what is coming. It shows he walked into his arrest on purpose rather than being caught off guard.
entries.14:43: Judas arrives with a crowd armed with weapons, sent by the religious leaders. The betrayal comes from one of Jesus' own twelve closest followers, not from strangers.
entries.14:44: Judas had arranged a kiss as the signal so the crowd would know which man to arrest. A friendly greeting was used to hand Jesus over, which makes the betrayal especially painful.
entries.14:45: Judas walks right up to Jesus, calls him Master, and kisses him. The sign was carried out exactly as planned, and Jesus was identified for arrest.
entries.14:46: The crowd grabs Jesus and takes him into custody. From this point he is a prisoner in the hands of his enemies.
entries.14:47: One of those standing nearby draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant. Someone tried to defend Jesus with violence, but it did not stop the arrest.
entries.14:48: Jesus points out the absurdity of a crowd coming with weapons to arrest him. He was not a dangerous criminal, yet they treated him like one.
entries.14:49: Jesus reminds them he taught openly in the Temple every day and they never seized him then. He says this is happening to fulfill what the Scriptures foretold.
entries.14:50: All of Jesus' followers run away in fear, leaving him alone. Even his closest friends abandoned him when trouble came.
entries.14:51: A young man wearing only a linen cloth was following along, and the crowd tried to grab him too. He was caught up in the danger surrounding Jesus.
entries.14:52: The young man escaped, leaving his cloth behind and running away naked. It shows how frantic and frightening the scene had become.
entries.14:53: Jesus is taken to the high priest, where the top religious leaders had gathered. His trial before the authorities begins.
entries.14:54: Peter followed at a safe distance and sat by the fire in the high priest's courtyard. He wanted to stay close to Jesus but not be identified with him.
entries.14:55: The religious leaders were trying to find evidence to justify putting Jesus to death, but they could not find any. They had already decided what they wanted and were hunting for a reason.
entries.14:56: Many people told lies about Jesus, but their stories did not match each other. Even false accusations failed to hold together.
entries.14:57: Some men stood up and gave false testimony against Jesus. They were willing to lie in order to get the outcome they wanted.
entries.14:58: They claimed Jesus said he would destroy the Temple and build another one in three days without hands. They twisted his words into a charge against him.
entries.14:59: Even these witnesses could not agree with each other. The case against Jesus kept falling apart.
entries.14:60: The high priest stands up and demands that Jesus answer the accusations. He is pressing Jesus to respond to the charges being made.
entries.14:61: Jesus stays silent and says nothing. Then the high priest asks him directly if he is the Messiah, the Son of God.
entries.14:62: Jesus answers clearly that he is, and says they will see him seated in power and coming with the clouds. He openly claims to be the Messiah, which is what leads to his condemnation.
entries.14:63: The high priest tears his clothes in shock and says no more witnesses are needed. He treats Jesus' answer as a shocking claim that settles the matter.
entries.14:64: The high priest calls Jesus' words blasphemy and asks the council for their verdict. They all agree he deserves to die.
entries.14:65: Some begin to spit on Jesus, blindfold him, hit him, and mockingly ask him to prophesy. The guards also strike him. He is humiliated and abused before his trial is even finished.
entries.14:66: While this was happening, Peter was down in the courtyard of the high priest's house. A servant girl came over to him.
entries.14:67: The servant girl looks at Peter by the fire and says he was with Jesus of Nazareth. She recognizes him as one of Jesus' followers.
entries.14:68: Peter denies knowing Jesus or understanding what she means, then moves out to the doorway. Just then a rooster crows.
entries.14:69: The girl sees Peter again and tells the people standing nearby that he is one of Jesus' followers. She repeats her accusation.
entries.14:70: Peter denies it again. A little later, the people nearby insist he must be one of them because his accent shows he is from Galilee.
entries.14:71: Peter calls down curses on himself and swears he does not know the man they are talking about. He denies Jesus a third time, more strongly than before.
entries.14:72: The rooster crows a second time, and Peter remembers Jesus' prediction that he would deny him three times. Realizing what he has done, he breaks down and weeps.
entries.15:1: Early in the morning the religious leaders met and decided to hand Jesus over to Pilate, the Roman governor. It shows how quickly and deliberately the leaders moved against him.
entries.15:2: Pilate asked Jesus directly if he claimed to be the king of the Jews, and Jesus answered in a way that neither denied nor fully admitted it. His calm reply sets the tone for how he faces the trial.
entries.15:3: The chief priests kept piling accusations against Jesus. The reader sees that many were speaking against him at once.
entries.15:4: Pilate pressed Jesus to answer the charges, pointing out how serious they were. He was surprised Jesus stayed so quiet.
entries.15:5: Jesus said nothing more, which amazed Pilate. His silence was striking and made Pilate wonder who he really was.
entries.15:6: It was the custom at the Passover feast for the governor to release one prisoner the crowd asked for. This sets up what happens next.
entries.15:7: A man named Barabbas was in prison for taking part in a rebellion and for murder. He was a violent criminal, not an innocent man.
entries.15:8: The crowd came to Pilate asking him to do what he usually did at the feast. They expected a prisoner to be released.
entries.15:9: Pilate asked the crowd if they wanted him to release Jesus, calling him the King of the Jews. He was offering them a choice.
entries.15:10: Pilate understood that the religious leaders had handed Jesus over because they were jealous of him. He saw their real motive.
entries.15:11: The chief priests stirred up the crowd to ask for Barabbas instead of Jesus. The crowd was turned against Jesus by their influence.
entries.15:12: Pilate asked the crowd what he should do with Jesus, the one they called the King of the Jews. He was still trying to find a way out.
entries.15:13: The crowd shouted back that Jesus should be crucified. Their demand was harsh and immediate.
entries.15:14: Pilate asked what crime Jesus had committed, but the crowd only shouted louder for his death. They had no real answer, just anger.
entries.15:15: Pilate wanted to please the crowd, so he released Barabbas and handed Jesus over to be whipped and crucified. He chose popularity over justice.
entries.15:16: The soldiers took Jesus into the courtyard of the governor's building and gathered the whole unit around him. He was now in their hands.
entries.15:17: The soldiers dressed Jesus in a purple robe and put a crown made of thorns on his head. They were mocking him as a fake king.
entries.15:18: The soldiers greeted Jesus as if he were a king, but they were making fun of him. Their words were sarcastic, not respectful.
entries.15:19: The soldiers hit Jesus on the head with a stick, spat on him, and knelt down pretending to honor him. It was cruel mockery of someone who had done nothing wrong.
entries.15:20: After they finished mocking Jesus, the soldiers put his own clothes back on him and led him out to be crucified. The abuse was over, but the execution was next.
entries.15:21: The soldiers forced a passerby named Simon from Cyrene to carry Jesus' cross. He was pulled into the story without choosing to be there.
entries.15:22: They brought Jesus to a place called Golgotha, which means the place of the skull. The name describes the grim location of his execution.
entries.15:23: They offered Jesus wine mixed with myrrh, a drink meant to dull the pain, but he refused it. He chose to face his suffering fully awake.
entries.15:24: The soldiers nailed Jesus to the cross and gambled for his clothes to decide who would get each piece. Even his few belongings were taken from him.
entries.15:25: It was about nine in the morning when they crucified Jesus. The text gives the specific time of his execution.
entries.15:26: A sign on the cross stated the charge against Jesus: that he claimed to be the King of the Jews. It was meant to mock him, but it told the truth about who he was.
entries.15:27: Two robbers were crucified alongside Jesus, one on each side. He died among criminals.
entries.15:28: This verse is not included in this translation, so there is nothing here to explain.
entries.15:29: People walking by insulted Jesus, shaking their heads and mocking his claim about destroying and rebuilding the temple. They twisted his words to make fun of him.
entries.15:30: The mockers told Jesus to save himself and come down from the cross. They challenged him to prove himself by escaping his suffering.
entries.15:31: The religious leaders laughed among themselves, saying Jesus saved others but could not save himself. They thought his helplessness proved he was not who he claimed to be.
entries.15:32: They challenged the Messiah, the King of Israel, to come down from the cross so they could believe. Even the two criminals crucified with him insulted him.
entries.15:33: At noon darkness covered the whole land until three in the afternoon. The darkness adds a sense of dread and sorrow to the scene.
entries.15:34: At three in the afternoon Jesus cried out loudly, asking God why he had been forsaken. He expressed real anguish and a sense of abandonment.
entries.15:35: Some nearby heard Jesus' cry and thought he was calling for the prophet Elijah. They misunderstood what he said.
entries.15:36: One person quickly soaked a sponge in sour wine, put it on a stick, and offered it to Jesus to drink, while others waited to see if Elijah would come. They were curious, not compassionate.
entries.15:37: Jesus gave a loud cry and died. His death is stated simply and directly.
entries.15:38: The temple curtain was torn in two from top to bottom. This signaled that the barrier between God and people was removed.
entries.15:39: The Roman officer standing near Jesus saw how he died and said that truly this man was a son of God. Even a pagan soldier recognized something extraordinary in Jesus' death.
entries.15:40: Some women were watching from a distance, including Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and Salome. They stayed near even when others had fled.
entries.15:41: These women had followed Jesus in Galilee and helped provide for his needs, and they had come with him all the way to Jerusalem. It shows that women were faithful supporters of Jesus throughout his ministry.
entries.15:42: It was late in the day on the day before the Sabbath, so preparations had to be made quickly before the day of rest began. This sets the scene for why Jesus' burial had to happen right away.
entries.15:43: Joseph, a respected and important man who was looking forward to God's kingdom, boldly asked Pilate for Jesus' body. His courage shows that even a person of high standing was willing to publicly identify with Jesus.
entries.15:44: Pilate was surprised that Jesus had already died, so he called the officer in charge to confirm it. This detail shows that Jesus' death was real and verified by the authorities.
entries.15:45: After the officer confirmed the death, Pilate gave Joseph permission to take the body. The official confirmation makes it clear that Jesus truly died.
entries.15:46: Joseph bought a linen cloth, took Jesus' body down, wrapped it, and laid it in a tomb cut out of rock, then rolled a stone over the entrance. This was a proper burial, fulfilling what was customary for the dead.
entries.15:47: Two women, Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses, watched where Jesus' body was laid. Their witness matters because they knew the exact location of the tomb.
entries.16:1: After the Sabbath rest was over, three women bought spices to anoint Jesus' body. This shows their love and devotion, and reminds us that faithful care for others often costs us something.
entries.16:2: They went to the tomb very early on Sunday morning, just as the sun was rising. Their eagerness to honor Jesus challenges us to seek him promptly and sincerely.
entries.16:3: On the way they worried about who would move the heavy stone blocking the tomb. It's natural to worry about obstacles, but God often handles them before we even arrive.
entries.16:4: When they looked, the huge stone was already rolled away. What seemed impossible to them had already been done, showing that God goes ahead of our concerns.
entries.16:5: Inside the tomb they saw a young man in a white robe sitting on the right, and they were startled. This was an angel, and his presence signals that something extraordinary from God was happening.
entries.16:6: The angel told them not to be afraid and announced that Jesus, who was crucified, had risen and was no longer there. The empty tomb is the heart of the Christian message: death did not hold Jesus.
entries.16:7: The angel sent the women to tell the disciples, including Peter, that Jesus would meet them in Galilee. Even Peter, who had denied Jesus, was included, showing that failure does not exclude us from Jesus' invitation.
entries.16:8: The women fled in fear and amazement and said nothing to anyone at first because they were terrified. Fear is a normal first reaction to God's power, but it doesn't have to be the final word.
entries.16:9: Jesus rose early on Sunday and appeared first to Mary Magdalene, a woman he had freed from seven demons. Jesus honors those who have been deeply rescued, and no past makes someone unworthy to meet him.
entries.16:10: Mary went and told the grieving, weeping followers of Jesus the news. She brought hope to people in sorrow, showing that the resurrection is meant to comfort those who mourn.
entries.16:11: When they heard that Jesus was alive and had been seen by Mary, they refused to believe it. Even close followers can struggle with doubt, so our doubts don't disqualify us from Jesus' care.
entries.16:12: Afterward Jesus appeared in a different form to two of them as they walked into the countryside. Jesus meets people in ordinary moments and in ways they don't immediately recognize.
entries.16:13: Those two returned and told the others, but they were not believed either. News of the resurrection was hard for people to accept, reminding us that faith often grows slowly.
entries.16:14: Later Jesus appeared to the eleven while they were eating and rebuked them for their stubborn unbelief and for not trusting those who had seen him. Jesus takes unbelief seriously, yet he still came to them rather than abandoning them.
entries.16:15: Jesus commanded his followers to go into all the world and share the good news with every person. This is the church's mission, and every believer is called to pass on the message of Jesus.
entries.16:16: Believing and being baptized brings salvation, while refusing to believe brings judgment. The key issue is trust in Jesus, and baptism is the outward step of that faith.
entries.16:17: Jesus said miraculous signs would accompany those who believe, such as driving out evil spirits and speaking in new languages. These signs confirm the message and show that God's power works through ordinary believers.
entries.16:18: Believers would handle snakes and drink poison without harm, and would heal the sick by laying hands on them. These promises show God's protection and healing power at work in the mission of his people.
entries.16:19: After speaking to them, Jesus was taken up into heaven and seated at God's right hand. This means Jesus now rules with full authority and continues to work on behalf of his people.
entries.16:20: The disciples went out and preached everywhere, and the Lord worked with them, confirming the message with signs. When we share the good news, Jesus himself works alongside us to make it effective.
